contentBlocks.body: A Python list is the closest match to a JavaScript array: ordered, mutable, and able to hold mixed types. append adds to the end (like push), pop removes from the end, and len(items) replaces items.length. Negative indices count from the end, so items[-1] is the last element.

contentBlocks.code:
items = [3, 1, 2]
items.append(4)      # [3, 1, 2, 4]
last = items.pop()   # 4
print(len(items))    # 3
print(items[-1])     # 2
print(sorted(items)) # [1, 2, 3]  (new list; items.sort() sorts in place)
print([1, 2] + [3])  # [1, 2, 3]

contentBlocks.body: A tuple is an immutable, ordered sequence written with parentheses. Use it for fixed groups such as coordinates or for returning several values from a function. Unpacking works like array destructuring, which makes swapping two variables a one-liner.

contentBlocks.code:
point = (3, 4)
x, y = point          # unpacking
a, b = 1, 2
a, b = b, a           # swap: a is 2, b is 1
single = (5,)         # the trailing comma makes it a tuple
# point[0] = 9        # TypeError: tuples cannot be changed

contentBlocks.body: Assignment never copies. After b = a, both names point at the same list, so b.append(1) changes a too. Copy with a.copy(), list(a) or a[:].

knowledgeItems.prompt: What does this print? a = [1, 2]; b = a; b.append(3); print(a)

payload.explanation: b = a makes both names refer to the same list object, just like with JavaScript arrays.
Parentheses alone just group an expression. A one-element tuple needs a trailing comma: (5,).
Index -1 is the last element (3) and -2 is the one before it (2).
